title: Finite State Machines: A Circuit That Remembers Where It Was
topic: Finite state machines — model sequential logic as a graph of states and labelled transitions; a Moore-style 11-detector with three states (S0, S1, S2) walks an input bit-stream and asserts its output whenever it has just seen two ones in a row

beats.narration: A digital circuit that remembers what just happened — how do we describe it?

elements.content: A circuit with memory — what is it remembering?

beats.narration: Draw a state graph. Three bubbles for three memory states, arrows labelled with the input bit that triggers each transition.

elements.content: Three state bubbles S0, S1, S2 arranged in a triangle
Transition arrows: S0 -1- S1, S1 -1- S2, S1 -0- S0, S2 -0- S0, S2 -1- S2 (self-loop), S0 -0- S0 (self-loop)
State annotations: S0=idle, S1=saw 1, S2=saw 11 (output high)

beats.narration: Feed a bitstream in, one bit per clock tick. The current state bubble lights up; the transition arrow pulses as the next bit decides where to go next.

elements.content: Bitstream row at the top — 0 1 1 0 1 1 1 0 — with a cursor sliding bit by bit
Same FSM graph below, with the active state glowing as the cursor advances
The just-fired transition arrow flashes on each tick

beats.narration: The output is high only when the machine is parked in S two — that means it has just seen two ones in a row.

elements.content: Output Z trace synchronously with the walked bitstream — high during the bits where the FSM sits in S2, zero elsewhere

beats.narration: States, transitions, outputs — that is every controller, every protocol, every counter you will ever build.

elements.content: (register holds the state, combinational logic fires transitions)
